# Soft tissue lesions of the shoulder

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Soft tissue lesions of the shoulder*

[Original Article Link](/library/UQ0bvf)

---

## Summary

<u>Soft tissue</u> lesions of the shoulder involve the shoulder's <u>ligaments</u>, <u>tendons</u>, <u>cartilage</u>, and/or capsule. The <u>rotator cuff</u> is the most commonly affected structure. <u>Rotator cuff disease</u> includes a range of pathologies from tendinopathy to <u>rotator cuff tears</u> and is commonly associated with <u>subacromial bursitis</u> and <u>biceps tendinopathy</u>. Many patients present with <u>subacromial impingement syndrome</u>, caused by inflammation of subacromial structures (e.g., <u>rotator cuff</u> <u>tendons</u>, <u>subacromial bursa</u>, and <u>long head of the biceps</u>) and subsequent narrowing of the subacromial space. Other frequently encountered <u>soft tissue</u> lesions of the shoulder include <u>adhesive capsulitis</u>, <u>calcific tendonitis</u>, and labral tears. <u>Soft tissue</u> lesions may result from overuse (e.g., repetitive <u>overhead</u> arm movements in young athletes) or degenerative or inflammatory processes. Symptoms of <u>soft tissue</u> lesions of the shoulder include <u>pain</u> with movement (usually shoulder <u>abduction</u>), nocturnal <u>pain</u>, tenderness, and/or restricted <u>range of motion</u> (<u>ROM</u>). A <u>clinical diagnosis</u> can often be made after an <u>orthopedic shoulder examination</u> that utilizes provocation tests for specific shoulder injuries. Imaging tests, primarily <u>MRI</u>, are usually obtained to make a definitive diagnosis and/or plan for <u>surgery</u>, if necessary. Management is typically conservative: activity modification, <u>NSAIDs</u>, and <u>physical therapy</u>. Intraarticular <u>corticosteroid</u> injections and/or <u>surgery</u> may be required if symptoms do not resolve with <u>conservative measures</u>. Early surgical intervention is indicated for labral tears causing instability and acute or large <u>rotator cuff tears</u>, especially in active individuals.




See also “<u>Biceps tendonitis</u>,” “<u>Subacromial bursitis</u>,” “<u>Acromioclavicular joint injury</u>,” and “<u>Shoulder dislocation</u>.”

---

## Overview

### General principles




* The majority of shoulder <u>pain</u> is the result of <u>rotator cuff disease</u>, a spectrum of pathophysiology ranging from <u>subacromial impingement</u> to complete tears of <u>rotator cuff</u> <u>tendons</u> (most commonly the <u>supraspinatus</u>).

* Other sources of <u>pain</u> include the: [[1]](/library/6lWjBl0)[[2]](/library/uOWp8l0)[[3]](/library/plWLBl0)

* <u>Biceps</u> <u>tendon</u>

* <u>Glenohumeral joint</u> capsule

* <u>Subacromial bursa</u>

* Acromioclavicular (AC) <u>joint</u>

* <u>Glenohumeral joint</u>





### Management approach [[4]](/library/FOWg8l0)[[5]](/library/OlWICl0)




* Perform a thorough <u>orthopedic shoulder examination</u>.

* Perform a <u>neurovascular examination</u> of the entire arm.

* Obtain standard <u>x-rays</u> in all patients. [[5]](/library/OlWICl0)[[6]](/library/rlWfyl0)

* Consider <u>MRI</u> or <u>ultrasound</u> imaging if the diagnosis remains unclear. [[6]](/library/rlWfyl0)[[7]](/library/IlWYyl0)

* Begin <u>conservative management</u>, unless there is an indication for <u>surgery</u>.

* Consult orthopedics urgently for the following: [[8]](/library/mNWVbN0)

* Suspected <u>joint</u> infection, e.g., warmth, red <u>skin</u>, systemic symptoms

* Unreduced <u>dislocation</u>

* Acute traumatic <u>rotator cuff tear</u>

* Mass on examination or imaging

> Always compare the affected shoulder to the <u>contralateral</u> shoulder when performing an <u>orthopedic shoulder examination</u>.

## Etiology

* Overuse: especially with activities involving repetitive <u>overhead</u> arm movement, e.g., baseball, volleyball

* Degenerative processes (especially in older individuals)

* Trauma

* Inflammation

* Systemic diseases (See “<u>Adhesive capsulitis</u>.”)

* Postoperative changes, e.g., inflammation, fibrous tissue, implants

---

## Clinical features

The following are nonspecific features. Provocative <u>clinical examination</u> and diagnostic tests are usually required to identify the underlying condition (see “<u>Overview of shoulder soft tissue lesions</u>).




* Painful active and/or passive <u>abduction</u>  [[4]](/library/FOWg8l0)[[5]](/library/OlWICl0)

* May be aggravated by internal and/or <u>external rotation</u>

* Localization of <u>pain</u> over the deltoid with shoulder <u>abduction</u> suggests <u>rotator cuff disease</u>.

* <u>Anterior</u> superior <u>pain</u> suggests <u>acromioclavicular joint</u> pathology.

* Patient apprehension before <u>shoulder movement</u>

* Tenderness, e.g., subacromial

* Limited <u>ROM</u> (active and/or passive)

* <u>Weakness</u>





![Normal range of shoulder abduction and pain in impingement](media/rcx2z7hmjeytbxepy489suiw.jpg)

Normal range of shoulder abduction and pain in impingement

---

## Diagnosis

The <u>clinical examination</u> can guide early management (see “<u>Overview of shoulder soft tissue lesions</u>”). Imaging is usually obtained to confirm the diagnosis and/or rule out alternative diagnoses. [[6]](/library/rlWfyl0)[[7]](/library/IlWYyl0)[[9]](/library/JlWsBl0)




### Clinical evaluation




* <u>Orthopedic shoulder examination</u> should include the following:

* <u>Shoulder mobility testing</u>

* <u>Shoulder impingement tests</u>

* <u>Shoulder instability tests</u>

* <u>Rotator cuff examination</u>

* <u>Proximal biceps tendon examination</u>

* <u>Neurovascular examination</u>

* Check upper extremity <u>capillary refill time</u> and pulses at the <u>radial artery</u>, <u>ulnar artery</u>, and <u>brachial artery</u>.

* Identify signs of <u>median nerve palsy</u>, <u>radial nerve palsy</u>, <u>ulnar nerve palsy</u>, or <u>axillary nerve palsy</u>.





### <u>X-ray</u>  [[6]](/library/rlWfyl0)[[7]](/library/IlWYyl0)




* Initial imaging for all patients

* Required views: standard AP, AP glenoid , trans-scapular <u>lateral</u> , and axillary [[11]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[17]](/library/zr1rPR0)

* Often normal

* Findings may include:

* Degenerative changes or narrowing of the subacromial space (e.g., due to structural abnormalities of the <u>acromion</u>)

* Calcification of the <u>supraspinatus</u> <u>tendon</u> in <u>calcifying tendinitis</u>

* Alternative causes of shoulder <u>pain</u> (e.g., <u>pathological fracture</u>)





![Shoulder X-ray](media/rwck2inyje39jwh45r7dd74d.jpg)

Shoulder X-ray

![Y view (lateral scapula view) of the shoulder](media/swrsysd61ormvxdtg3oy2z70.jpg)

Y view (lateral scapula view) of the shoulder




### <u>MRI</u>  [[6]](/library/rlWfyl0)




* <u>Gold standard</u> imaging for evaluation of the shoulder

* Indications: diagnostic uncertainty or symptoms that persist following <u>conservative treatment</u>

* Supports surgical planning





![Normal MRI left shoulder region](media/ffi4i5hhbzhxxt9g8fzvvgk4.jpg)

Normal MRI left shoulder region




### <u>Ultrasound</u> [[18]](/library/zqWra50)




* Provides real-time imaging during provocation maneuvers and is used to guide interventional treatment

* <u>Accuracy</u> comparable to <u>MRI</u> for <u>rotator cuff tears</u>, <u>bursitis</u>, and other shoulder <u>soft tissue</u> lesions [[9]](/library/JlWsBl0)[[19]](/library/uIWpe50)

* Findings may include:

* Damage to the <u>soft tissue</u> structures (<u>bursae</u>, <u>rotator cuff</u> <u>tendons</u>)

* Bicep <u>tendon</u> rupture, subluxation, or <u>dislocation</u> (e.g., acromioclavicular or <u>glenohumeral joints</u>)

---

## Treatment

The majority of patients with <u>soft tissue</u> injuries of the shoulder can be managed initially with <u>conservative therapy</u>. [[5]](/library/OlWICl0)[[20]](/library/8OWO8l0)




### Conservative therapy of shoulder soft tissue lesions




* Utilize the <u>POLICE principle</u> for acute injuries or inflammation.

* <u>Manage acute pain</u>, e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>.

* Modify activities, especially those involving <u>overhead</u> movements.

* Consult <u>physical therapy</u>.

* Consider subacromial <u>glucocorticoid</u> injections for refractory <u>chronic pain</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Adequate <u>pain control</u> is necessary to optimize the results of <u>physical therapy</u>. [[21]](/library/EUW8Uk0)




> [!WARNING]
> Wait at least 4 months between <u>glucocorticoid</u> injections to avoid weakening the <u>tendons</u>. [[5]](/library/OlWICl0)




### Surgical treatment




* Indications [[5]](/library/OlWICl0)

* Acute injury with full-thickness <u>rotator cuff tear</u> and/or <u>shoulder dislocation</u>

* Acute labral injuries with recurrent <u>shoulder dislocation</u> [[22]](/library/FMWgqN0)[[23]](/library/8MWOqN0)

* Chronic full-thickness <u>rotator cuff tear</u>(s) in individuals < 65 years of age

* Symptoms that persist after 3–6 months of <u>conservative treatment</u> [[20]](/library/8OWO8l0)

* Technique: depends on the specific condition

* <u>Arthroscopic</u> <u>surgery</u>, e.g., decompression of <u>subacromial impingement</u>

* Open arthrotomy, e.g., open <u>rotator cuff</u> repair

* Manipulation under anesthesia, e.g., for <u>adhesive capsulitis</u>

---

## Subacromial impingement syndrome

### Background




* Definition

* A syndrome of <u>pain</u> during shoulder <u>abduction</u>, forward <u>flexion</u>, and/or extreme <u>adduction</u> associated with narrowing of the subacromial space

* Encompasses a spectrum of pathologies, including <u>rotator cuff disease</u>, <u>subacromial bursitis</u>, and <u>biceps tendinopathy</u> [[2]](/library/uOWp8l0)

* Etiology: repetitive <u>overhead</u> activity or other overuse injuries

* Pathophysiology [[2]](/library/uOWp8l0)

* Extrinsic compression: Narrowed subacromial space causes <u>bursitis</u> and <u>tendonitis</u>.

* Intrinsic compression: Degenerative <u>tendonitis</u> causes glenohumeral changes that narrow the subacromial space.

* Stages
1. * Degeneration leads to the formation of <u>edema</u> and bleeding in the area of the <u>rotator cuff</u> <u>tendons</u> and <u>subacromial bursa</u>.
2. * <u>Fibrosis</u> of the <u>bursa</u>
3. * <u>Tendon</u> tear or rupture, intermittent <u>bursitis</u>, and pseudoparalysis of the arm





### Clinical features




* <u>Pain</u> on movement that is worsened by <u>overhead</u> activities (e.g., combing <u>hair</u> or reaching up to a cupboard)

* Nocturnal exacerbation of <u>pain</u>, especially when lying on the affected shoulder

* <u>Pain</u> and restriction of active movement between 60 and 120°

* Symptoms typically develop over weeks to months. [[24]](/library/KB1Ubj0)





![Normal range of shoulder abduction and pain in impingement](media/rcx2z7hmjeytbxepy489suiw.jpg)

Normal range of shoulder abduction and pain in impingement




### Diagnosis [[2]](/library/uOWp8l0)




Can be <u>diagnosed clinically</u>




* Positive provocative <u>clinical examination</u>

* <u>Neer test</u>

* <u>Hawkins test</u>

* <u>Painful arc test</u>

* <u>X-rays</u>: may show narrowing of acromiohumeral distance, <u>osteoarthritis</u>

* <u>MRI</u>: provides definitive evidence of <u>tendinitis</u> and/or impingement [[24]](/library/KB1Ubj0)

* Subacromial lidocaine injection test [[25]](/library/rbYfEn)[[26]](/library/pMWLpN0)

* Indication: inability to differentiate between <u>subacromial impingement syndrome</u> and other causes of shoulder <u>pain</u> and/or restricted <u>ROM</u>, e.g., <u>rotator cuff tear</u>, <u>frozen shoulder</u>, <u>glenohumeral joint</u> <u>arthritis</u>  [[27]](/library/TPX6Vy)

* Technique: subacromial injection of 5 mL of <u>lidocaine</u> or <u>bupivacaine</u> [[26]](/library/pMWLpN0)

* Interpretation: <u>Pain</u> relief following injection suggests <u>subacromial impingement syndrome</u>.





![Impingement Syndrome - Neer Test](media/small_6075509a75138.jpg)

Impingement Syndrome - Neer Test

![Impingement Syndrome - Painful Arc Test - Clinical Examination](media/small_6075507e786ca.jpg)

Impingement Syndrome - Painful Arc Test - Clinical Examination




### Treatment [[2]](/library/uOWp8l0)




* All patients: Begin <u>conservative therapy of shoulder soft tissue lesions</u>.

* Surgical treatment: if there is no improvement after <u>conservative treatment</u> (e.g., <u>arthroscopic</u> decompression, acromioplasty)





### Complications




* <u>Adhesive capsulitis</u>

* Otherwise dependent on underlying pathology

* See “<u>Rotator cuff disease</u>.”

* See “<u>Subacromial bursitis</u>.”

* See “<u>Biceps tendinopathy</u>.”





![Subacromial impingement syndrome](media/hgxg20fom7oacta8n0y6atw4.jpg)

Subacromial impingement syndrome

## Rotator cuff disease

### General principles [[28]](/library/9OWNul0)[[29]](/library/7114Rf0)




* <u>Rotator cuff disease</u> is a poorly defined collection of traumatic injuries and/or degenerative changes to <u>rotator cuff</u> <u>tendons</u>.

* It includes a spectrum of conditions ranging from <u>tendonitis</u> to <u>rotator cuff tears</u>.

* Comorbid adjacent lesions are common, e.g., <u>subacromial bursitis</u>, <u>biceps tendinopathy</u>.

* Clinical features vary depending on the underlying conditions and course.

* <u>Subacromial impingement syndrome</u> is a common (but not universal) manifestation of <u>rotator cuff tendinopathy</u> and <u>calcific tendonitis of the shoulder</u>.

* Loss of active <u>rotator cuff</u> function suggests a <u>rotator cuff tear</u>.





### Rotator cuff tendinopathy [[29]](/library/7114Rf0)[[30]](/library/FkWgpl0)




* Definition

* Inflammatory and/or degenerative changes of one or more <u>rotator cuff</u> <u>tendons</u>

* Encompasses the spectrum of <u>rotator cuff disease</u> between impingement and <u>rotator cuff tear</u>

* Etiology: acute injury and/or chronic degeneration from overuse

* Clinical features

* Can present as <u>subacromial impingement syndrome</u>

* Subacromial tenderness on palpation

* <u>Referred pain</u> in the deltoid area with <u>overhead</u> activities

* Possible <u>atrophy</u> of the <u>supraspinatus</u> and <u>infraspinatus</u> muscles

* Diagnosis [[30]](/library/FkWgpl0)

* Often a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on provocation testing

* <u>Painful arc test</u> (early finding)

* <u>Empty can test</u>

* <u>Infraspinatus test</u>

* <u>Belly press test</u>

* <u>MRI</u> or <u>ultrasound</u> findings provide a definitive diagnosis.

* Treatment: : Follow <u>conservative therapy of shoulder soft tissue lesions</u>.

* Complications  [[28]](/library/9OWNul0)

* Muscle <u>atrophy</u> or fatty degeneration

* <u>Rotator cuff tear</u>, rupture, and/or <u>retraction</u>

* <u>Adhesive capsulitis</u>

### Rotator cuff tear




<u>Rotator cuff tears</u> are often preceded by <u>rotator cuff tendonitis</u> and most commonly involve the <u>supraspinatus</u> <u>tendon</u>.   [[31]](/library/i6WJkm0)




* Etiology [[28]](/library/9OWNul0)[[29]](/library/7114Rf0)

* Chronic degenerative tear (most common): usually seen in individuals > 40 years of age and/or performing repetitive <u>overhead</u> movements (e.g., <u>infraspinatus</u> tear in baseball pitchers) [[11]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Acute traumatic injury (∼ 10% of cases): usually seen following a fall or <u>dislocation</u>, often in young adults [[11]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Clinical features [[11]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Acute rupture: sudden severe <u>pain</u> and loss of strength

* Degenerative rupture: <u>chronic pain</u>; loss of strength is less pronounced than with acute tear

* Restricted active <u>ROM</u> (especially if passive <u>ROM</u> is normal)

* Diagnostics [[6]](/library/rlWfyl0)

* Positive <u>drop-arm test</u> suggests <u>supraspinatus</u> tear.

* Provocation tests that may be abnormal (depending on the affected <u>tendon</u>)

* <u>Empty can test</u>

* <u>Lift-off test</u>

* <u>Belly press test</u>

* <u>Infraspinatus test</u>

* <u>POCUS</u>: may show full or partial-thickness tears [[11]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>X-ray</u>: superior displacement of the <u>humeral head</u> (high-riding <u>humeral head</u>)

* <u>Ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u>: definitive test to determine the location and extent of the rupture

* Treatment

* All patients: Optimize <u>conservative therapy of shoulder soft tissue lesions</u>.

* Acute injury: Immobilize for comfort and consult orthopedic <u>surgery</u> early.

* Surgical repair ;  [[5]](/library/OlWICl0)[[32]](/library/Q6Wukm0)[[33]](/library/EIW8e50)

* Typically considered for: 

* Younger patients (< 65 years old) with:

* Acute traumatic full-thickness tears

* Chronic full-thickness tears  [[33]](/library/EIW8e50)

* Significantly reduced arm function

* High risk of tear progression

* Insufficient improvement after 3–6 months of <u>conservative treatment</u> [[20]](/library/8OWO8l0)

* Typically inappropriate for:

* Sedentary and older patients (> 65 years)  [[5]](/library/OlWICl0)

* Most partial-thickness tears

* Complications

* Tear progression [[5]](/library/OlWICl0)

* <u>Adhesive capsulitis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Early surgical repair of a <u>rotator cuff tear</u> is often preferred in young and/or physically active patients. [[11]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[34]](/library/j6W_km0)

### Calcific tendonitis of the shoulder [[13]](/library/UlWbwl0)[[14]](/library/2lWTwl0)




* Etiology: See “<u>Calcific tendonitis</u>” in “<u>BCP crystal deposition diseases</u>.”

* Clinical features

* Primarily affects <u>rotator cuff</u> <u>tendons</u> causing features similar to <u>rotator cuff tendinopathy</u>.

* Can occasionally affect the <u>long head of the biceps</u> (see “<u>Biceps tendonitis</u>.”)

* Diagnosis

* <u>X-rays</u> usually show <u>calcium</u> deposits.

* <u>Ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u> are diagnostic but not required if <u>calcium</u> deposits are seen on <u>x-ray</u>. [[13]](/library/UlWbwl0)

* Treatment

* Follow <u>conservative therapy of shoulder soft tissue lesions</u>.  [[13]](/library/UlWbwl0)

* Physical removal of <u>calcium</u> deposits may be considered if symptoms persist after 6 months of <u>conservative management</u>. [[14]](/library/2lWTwl0)[[35]](/library/EOW88l0)

* Percutaneous <u>ultrasound</u>-guided barbotage of crystals

* <u>Arthroscopic</u> <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Extracorporeal shock wave therapy</u>

## Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)

* Definition: inflammation and <u>fibrosis</u> of the <u>joint capsule</u> leading to <u>contracture</u> of the <u>shoulder joint</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[36]](/library/tkWXpl0)

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* Onset > 40 years of age

* Etiology [[15]](/library/KlWUBl0)[[16]](/library/0lWevl0)[[37]](/library/9lWN_l0)

* Primary <u>adhesive capsulitis</u> (<u>idiopathic</u>): associated with <u>diabetes mellitus</u>, <u>thyroid disorders</u>, <u>scleroderma</u>, <u>Dupuytren contracture</u>, <u>ASCVD</u>

* Secondary <u>adhesive capsulitis</u>: associated with previous shoulder injury (e.g., <u>shoulder dislocation</u>, <u>rotator cuff disease</u>), prolonged <u>immobilization</u>, <u>arthroscopic</u> <u>surgery</u>

* Stages
1. * <u>Freezing</u> or painful stage: minimal <u>synovitis</u> with <u>pain</u>, causing a limitation of <u>ROM</u>
2. * Frozen or transitional stage: <u>Pain</u> decreases, but <u>synovitis</u> continues (with axillary adhesions and contraction of the capsule).
3. * Thawing stage: Inflammation decreases and movement slowly improves.

* Clinical features [[11]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[36]](/library/tkWXpl0)[[38]](/library/ZIWZY50)

* Shoulder <u>pain</u> 

* Most commonly involves the nondominant side

* May be poorly localized; sometimes <u>pain</u> is referred to the deltoid and bicep

* More severe at night

* Stiffness that interferes with <u>activities of daily living</u>

* Severe restriction of active and passive <u>ROM</u> of the <u>glenohumeral joint</u> in all planes, especially:

* <u>External rotation</u>

* Passive <u>abduction</u> (restricted to < 90°)

* Diagnosis

* Can be <u>diagnosed clinically</u>

* <u>X-rays</u> are usually obtained to rule out underlying pathology.

* <u>MRI</u> provides a definitive diagnosis but is typically not required.

* Treatment [[36]](/library/tkWXpl0)[[37]](/library/9lWN_l0)

* <u>Physical therapy</u>: early mobilization and exercise

* <u>NSAIDs</u>

* Oral <u>corticosteroid</u> (burst and taper) for severe <u>pain</u>

* <u>Intraarticular corticosteroid injection</u>

* Surgical treatment if symptoms persist after 9 months of <u>conservative management</u>  [[11]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Prognosis: <u>self-limiting</u> (improvement typically takes > 1 year)

* Complications: <u>atrophy</u> of the deltoid and spinatus muscles
